original_title: Lanterns finally gives us the buddy cop show we were promised, but still won't give us what we want
summary_en: After weeks of anticipation, the latest episode of Lanterns leans into the dynamic duo energy fans have been waiting for. However, the show's signature melancholy still lingers, even with a resurrected mentor.

en.title: Lanterns Finally Delivers the Buddy Cop Vibes We Craved
en.summary: After weeks of anticipation, the latest episode of Lanterns leans into the dynamic duo energy fans have been waiting for. However, the show's signature melancholy still lingers, even with a resurrected mentor.
en.body:
For a series that promised the electrifying chemistry of a seasoned Green Lantern mentoring a younger, perhaps more reckless, counterpart, **Lanterns** has taken its sweet time delivering. But "The Jordan Boys" finally gives us the buddy cop show we were teased, albeit with a spectral twist. The resurrection of **Hal Jordan**, not as a living being but as a 'Halogram,' allows **Kyle Chandler** to shed the decade of pain that has burdened his character and present a version of Hal that feels more akin to the adventurous spirit fans know from the comics. This isn't the weary, broken man we've seen; this is a Hal who is confused and angry about his fate, yet not yet entirely crushed by it. It’s a more *fun* kind of reckless, a necessary injection of energy into the series' prevailing tone of regret and loss.

The dynamic between this Halogram and **John Stewart** is where the episode truly shines. The trailers hinted at this veteran-rookie banter, and the reality doesn't disappoint. John, blessedly able to silence his mentor with a mere thought or a blast of Outkast, finds a welcome relief in being able to finally shut up the stubbornly insistent Hal. Hal, the cheeky, wiseass veteran, completes the buddy cop equation, but his spectral existence and shock at John's revelations about his fate provide **Kyle Chandler** with ample room to explore a complex characterization. It’s a performance that balances the expected swagger with the profound disorientation of being a ghost in your own story.

## The Heart of the Matter

Beyond the central duo, the episode continues to weave in the threads of civilian life and its intersection with the extraordinary. **Kerry** finds herself in the unenviable position of managing the town's volatile reaction to yet another Green Lantern crisis, all while preparing for a significant family event – a party celebrating **Noah's** college football decision. **Kelly Macdonald** has been a standout, grounding the more fantastical elements of the story. Her character's role as the non-superpowered anchor in the central trio is crucial, providing a relatable perspective amidst the cosmic drama. The tension between maintaining normalcy and confronting alien threats is palpable, a testament to the show's commitment to exploring the human cost of being a Lantern.

## Fan Expectations Met, But Not Fulfilled?

Fans have been clamoring for the return of the classic Green Lantern dynamic, and "The Jordan Boys" certainly delivers on that front. The sheer fun of watching **Hal** and **John** bicker and strategize is undeniable. Yet, the source material's inherent melancholy, the theme of time irrevocably lost and the weight of responsibility, still permeates every scene. While we get the *buddy cop* show we were promised, the show seems reluctant to fully let go of its more somber exploration of grief and consequence. This duality, while compelling, leaves a lingering question: will **Lanterns** ever give us the unadulterated adventure we’ve been craving, or will it always be tinged with regret?

## What's Next

With **Hal Jordan** now a spectral presence, the implications for John's mission and the future of the Green Lantern Corps are immense. Viewers will be eager to see how this unique partnership evolves and what new threats emerge from the shadows of the universe.

content_raw: It makes sense that Lanterns could only give us what we wanted once one of the main characters was dead. “The Jordan Boys” plays with those expectations—and meets them—while maintaining the series’ tone of regret and loss and time irrevocably gone.  Hal Jordan is back in the form of the Halogram, this version allowing Kyle Chandler to shed a decade’s worth of pain to present a Hal more in line with the adventurer comics fans are used to. He’s reckless, refusing to help John break into The Fortress Of Storage until he gets to see Kerry, but it’s a more fun kind of reckless. Freed from his 10-year dormancy only to peer down into his own grave, this Hal is confused and pissed off, certainly. But he’s also not yet crushed and defensive and, well, afraid.  The dynamic between the Halogram and John bristles with the sort of crotchety banter the trailers deceptively frontloaded. John is blessedly relieved that he can finally shut his mentor up just by wishing it, realizing that he can banish the stubbornly insistent Hal by belting out some Outkast . Hal is the cheeky wiseass veteran Lantern—completing the whole buddy cop dynamic promos for the show teased us with—but his position as someone not quite alive (and fully shocked by John’s revelations about his fate) leaves Chandler acres to stretch out his characterization.  And then there’s Kerry, trying to keep a lid on the town’s volatile reaction to having another Green Lantern situation in its midst, all while preparing to host 100 people at her house for a party celebrating Noah’s hyped up college football decision. Kelly Macdonald’s been outstanding, even if Kerry’s status as the non-super of the central trio shunted her aside more than her male colleagues. But watch her eyes in the scene where John, blackmailed into introducing Hal’s “ghost,” tries to prepare her. If there’s a way to play a scene where someone channels the mix of emotion you feel when your dead lover (for whom you have deeply complicated feelings) appears in front of you while clearly not being the exact person you knew, then Kelly Macdonald finds it here. (The little flinch after she reaches out to touch Hal’s face is eloquently heartbreaking.)  The Halogram asks John on the way to meet Kerry, “I was in jail? I was in love?,” and the second question registers as more inconceivable than the first. Chandler, too, is remarkable in “The Jordan Boys,” tiptoeing the Halogram through a tangle of thoughts and emotions only a sci-fi scenario can truly create. The Halogram (I’m just calling him “Hal” from now on), is stubborn, ornery and filled with pain the likes of which the episode finally reveals.
